common_name: Kirschkönigin Yarrow (Cherry Queen Yarrow, Galaxy Series)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring once soil has warmed, in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Kirschkönigin, one of the German Galaxy-series hybrids, opens deep cherry-red and gradually softens through dusty rose before fading to cream as each flat-topped flower cluster ages, so a single plant often shows several shades at once. Grow in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; overly rich or damp soil produces weak, floppy stems and shortens the plant's life. Shear off spent flower heads to encourage rebloom and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring. Established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted in and draw bees, hoverflies, and butterflies over a long summer bloom season.

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring once soil has warmed, in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Credo carries broad, flat-topped clusters of soft primrose-yellow flowers that fade to buttery cream as they age, held above finely divided, ferny gray-green foliage on sturdy upright stems. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun, since fertile or overly moist ground causes lanky, weak-stemmed growth prone to flopping. Deadhead to extend the summer bloom period and to prevent unwanted self-seeding, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep plants vigorous. Its soft coloring blends easily in naturalistic and cottage-style plantings and draws bees and butterflies throughout the bloom season.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or set out transplants in spring, in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; give this species extra room, since it is considerably taller and coarser than most garden globe thistle cultivars.

directions: The straight species behind many garden globe thistle cultivars, Echinops sphaerocephalus is a tall, coarse-textured perennial bearing pale grayish-white to dusty steel-blue flower spheres on stiff, felted stems above spiny, deeply lobed gray-green leaves. Plant in poor to average, sharply drained soil in full sun; rich or damp ground encourages sprawling growth and can shorten its lifespan. Stake or grow among sturdy neighbors in exposed sites, since mature clumps are top-heavy in bloom. The globular flower heads are a strong late-summer draw for bumblebees and other pollinators, and this species self-sows readily, so deadhead spent heads before seed set where volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

common_name: Picos Blue Sea Holly (Compact Silver-Veined Pyrenean Eryngo)

planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed, since the long taproot resents disturbance once established.

directions: Picos Blue forms a low rosette of glossy, deeply cut leaves marbled with striking silvery-white veins, above which wiry stems carry small steel-blue flower cones ringed by spiny, blue-tinted bracts from midsummer into fall. Choose a lean, gritty, sharply drained site in full sun, since rich or waterlogged soil produces soft growth and dulls the leaf variegation. Leave winter mulch off the crown in cold climates, as excess moisture around the roots does more harm than the cold. Its compact habit suits rock gardens, gravel plantings, and the front of a border, and the flowers are a reliable draw for bees and other pollinators.

planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed, since the long taproot resents disturbance once established.

directions: Three-Lobed Sea Holly sends up a haze of wiry, branching, amethyst-tinted stems studded with small egg-shaped flower cones and fine spiny bracts, giving established clumps an airy, see-through quality prized in naturalistic and prairie-style plantings. Grow in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, since fertile or wet ground leads to floppy growth and rot. Its slender, open habit lets it thread through neighboring perennials and ornamental grasses without overwhelming them, and the small violet-blue flower heads bloom over an especially long summer-into-fall window. Bees and other pollinators visit heavily, and the dried seed heads provide winter interest if left standing.

planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed, since the long taproot resents disturbance once established.

directions: Moroccan Sea Holly forms a neat, evergreen rosette of rounded, leathery leaves etched with fine white veins, a feature that gives year-round interest even before the branching stems of small pale blue-gray flower cones appear in summer. Plant in lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; this species is more tolerant of light shade than most sea hollies but still needs excellent drainage to avoid crown rot over winter. Its compact size and patterned foliage make it a good choice for edging, gravel gardens, and containers. The flowers attract bees and other pollinators, and the foliage rosettes stay attractive through winter in milder climates.

common_name: Superbum Alpine Sea Holly (Large-Bracted Alpine Eryngo)

planting.note: Set out after the soil has warmed, since the long taproot resents disturbance once established.

directions: Superbum bears the largest, showiest flower heads of the alpine sea hollies, each steel-blue cone surrounded by a soft, feathery ruff of finely divided, silvery-blue bracts that give the flowers an almost thistledown-like texture. Grow in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; unlike many sea hollies it tolerates slightly richer, moisture-retentive ground without becoming floppy, though sharp drainage in winter is still important. The long-lasting flower heads are excellent for cutting and drying and hold their color well after harvest. Bees and other pollinators visit the flowers freely from midsummer into early fall.
